units.title: Proof habits and shape notation
outcomes: Translate a linear-algebra claim between prose, quantifiers, indexed sums and explicit shapes.
Prove an implication in both directions when needed, and identify where its assumptions enter.
Use contradiction, induction or a small counterexample rather than treating numerical tests as proofs.
units.why: A correct calculation can still answer the wrong quantified question. Proof habits make the assumptions behind every later decomposition and solver visible.

next.note: Use definitions to prove linearity and independence.
Apply quantifier discipline to asymptotic bounds.

study.title: Mathematics for Computer Science: proof templates and notation
study.locator: Lehman, Leighton and Meyer, Chapter 1, sections 1.1 to 1.9 (pp. 5 to 19); Chapter 3, sections 3.1 (pp. 42 to 45) and 3.6 (pp. 56 to 61); sections 4.1 to 4.4 (pp. 81 to 93)
study.depth: In Chapter 4, read the definitions of sets, sequences, functions and relations. Leave cardinality and the remaining logical-circuit material.

study.title: Induction and invariants
study.locator: Chapter 5, sections 5.1 to 5.3 (pp. 115 to 130), then 5.4.1 to 5.4.3 (pp. 130 to 135)
study.depth: Read the ordinary and strong induction templates and the robot invariant. Stop before the later state-machine applications.

study.title: Vectors, matrices and indexed products
study.locator: Chapter 2, section 2.2 (pp. 22 to 27), especially matrix multiplication, equation (2.11)
study.depth: Use this as notation repair, not a second first pass. Treat a tensor here as an array with an ordered list of axis sizes; multilinear tensor theory is outside this unit.

focus: Declare domains before quantifiers. Negating 'for every x, P(x)' gives 'there exists x with not P(x)', not 'every x fails'.
Separate an implication, its converse and its contrapositive. An iff requires both directions.
For A of shape (m,n), write (Ax)_i = sum_j A_ij x_j with x in R^n. Distinguish a scalar, a vector, a column matrix and an array with extra axes.
An induction proof needs a starting case and a step for every permitted index. An invariant needs initialization and preservation.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, prove that the columns a_1,...,a_n of a real m by n matrix A are independent iff Ax=0 has only x=0, using Ax=sum_j x_j a_j in both directions. Then prove (A^k)^T=(A^T)^k for square A and all integers k>=0, starting with A^0=I and using the transpose-of-product rule in the step. As one NumPy check, create A=np.array([[1,2],[2,4]],dtype=np.float64) and z=np.array([-2,1],dtype=np.float64), with no random draws. Compute np.linalg.norm(A@z,2): the reference run gives 0.0, below 1e-12. The nonzero witness z refutes independence for this A; the numerical check does not prove the general iff.
traps: Checking several vectors cannot establish a claim about all real vectors. One exact counterexample can refute it.
Swapping 'for every b there exists x' with 'there exists x for every b' changes solvability into a much stronger claim.
A vector of mathematical shape n is not automatically a NumPy (n,1) column. Write the storage shape separately.

selfTest.q: Where do the assumptions enter the independence iff proof?
selfTest.a: A has n columns in R^m, so Ax is the same linear combination used in the definition. Independence forces all coefficients x_j to vanish in the forward direction. In the reverse direction, the assumed trivial kernel forces the coefficients of any zero combination to vanish. Neither direction requires A to be square.

selfTest.q: Negate: for every b in R^m there exists x in R^n with Ax=b.
selfTest.a: There exists b in R^m such that for every x in R^n, Ax is not b. This is one unattainable right-hand side, not a statement that every b is unattainable.

selfTest.q: Why does the transpose-power induction start at zero, and what does its step use?
selfTest.a: For square A, A^0=I and I^T=I establish k=0. If the claim holds at k, then (A^(k+1))^T=(A^k A)^T=A^T(A^k)^T=A^T(A^T)^k=(A^T)^(k+1). Squareness makes the powers defined; the induction hypothesis is used at the third equality.

selfTest.q: Is T(x)=x+c linear for a fixed nonzero vector c?
selfTest.a: No. Every linear map sends zero to zero, but T(0)=c. Nonzero c is the assumption used to obtain the contradiction.

practice.name: 6.042J text: Problem 1.3(a), a bogus inequality proof
practice.note: Identify the first invalid step and repair the direction of the inequality. Then annotate the two linear-algebra proofs in reproduce with the assumption used at each step.

units.stopWhen: You can write the iff and transpose-power proofs without notes, negate the solvability claim with the domains intact, and explain why the NumPy witness is a refutation rather than a universal proof.

fit.note: The proof companion supplies checked templates and a named proof-debugging problem; MML supplies the matrix notation. Narrowed readings keep this within six hours.

units.title: Linear maps, span, independence and change of basis
outcomes: Construct a matrix representation from the images of an ordered basis and derive the matrix for a composition.
Distinguish spanning, independence and being a basis, including uniqueness of coordinates.
Derive the change-of-coordinates formula with separate input and output bases.
units.why: Coordinates describe a vector; they are not the vector itself. Keeping that distinction prevents wrong transposes and explains why a better basis can simplify the same map.

next.note: Describe what the map reaches and what it loses.
Apply the distinction between the map and its coordinate representation.

study.title: Independence and matrix representations
study.locator: Video Lecture 9, Independence, basis, and dimension; Lecture 30, Linear transformations and their matrices; Lecture 31, Change of basis; image compression
study.depth: In Lecture 31, stop after change of basis; leave image compression for SVD. These are video numbers, not calendar session numbers.

study.title: Basis change as a composition
study.locator: Chapter 2, sections 2.5 to 2.6 (pp. 40 to 48) for definitions, then 2.7.1 to 2.7.2 (pp. 50 to 58), especially Theorem 2.20 and its proof on pp. 54 to 55
study.depth: Read the basis-change proof line by line. Leave kernel/image in 2.7.3 for the next unit.

focus: Spanning gives existence of coordinates; independence gives uniqueness. Both are needed for a basis.
Column j is the output coordinate vector of the image of input basis vector j. Composition acts right to left on column vectors.
If x_old=S x_new and y_old=T y_new, then the new representation is T^(-1) A S. Only an endomorphism with the same basis change at both ends gives S^(-1) A S.
units.reproduce: Derive T^(-1)AS by following coordinates through three maps. By hand take A=diag(2,1), S=[[1,1],[0,1]], T=[[1,0],[1,1]] and obtain C=[[2,2],[-2,-1]]. For new input z=(1,2), compute old input (3,2), old output (6,2), and new output (6,-4). Check once in NumPy: create these arrays with dtype=np.float64, without random draws; compute C=np.linalg.solve(T,A@S) and np.linalg.norm(T@(C@z)-A@(S@z),2). The reference difference is 0.0; require it below 1e-12 rather than asserting floating-point equality.
traps: S contains the new basis vectors in old coordinates, not the reverse conversion. The inverse belongs on the output conversion.
A spanning list may contain redundant vectors. Its coefficients need not be unique.
An affine map with a nonzero offset is not a linear map even when implemented with a matrix multiplication.

selfTest.q: Why does a basis give unique coordinates?
selfTest.a: Spanning gives at least one expansion. Subtracting two expansions gives a zero linear combination. Independence forces every difference of coefficients to be zero. The two basis assumptions are used in different steps.

selfTest.q: For f(x)=Ax and g(y)=By, which matrix represents g composed with f?
selfTest.a: BA: g(f(x))=B(Ax). If A is m by n, B must have m columns; with B of shape p by m the result is p by n.

selfTest.q: Why is using S^T instead of S^(-1) wrong in general?
selfTest.a: A basis matrix need only be invertible, not orthogonal. For S=[[1,1],[0,1]], S^T=[[1,0],[1,1]], while S^(-1)=[[1,-1],[0,1]]. Only orthonormal basis columns imply S^T=S^(-1).

practice.name: MML Exercise 2.20: two input bases and a linear map
practice.locator: Chapter 2, Exercise 2.20(a) to (f), printed pp. 68 to 69
practice.note: Draw the two bases and solve the coordinate conversions before multiplying matrices. Part (f) checks the same output by two coordinate routes.

units.stopWhen: You solve Exercise 2.20 through its two output routes and can derive the order T^(-1)AS without memorizing it.

fit.note: 18.06 gives the first pass; MML provides a complete basis-change proof and a named exercise with an independent coordinate-route check.

units.title: The four subspaces, rank and solution sets
outcomes: Find bases for all four fundamental subspaces and state their ambient spaces and dimensions.
Prove rank-nullity and the orthogonal-complement relations for a real matrix.
Describe every solution of Ax=b and distinguish existence from identifiability of x.
units.why: Rank tells you which outputs are reachable and which parameter changes leave outputs unchanged. These are different failure modes, even before fitting data.

next.note: Project an unattainable right-hand side onto the column space.
Diagnose non-identifiable coefficients in an applied design matrix.

study.title: Null spaces, solution sets and the four subspaces
study.locator: Video Lectures 6 to 8, Column space and nullspace through Solving Ax=b; Lecture 10, The four fundamental subspaces; Lecture 14, Orthogonal vectors and subspaces
study.depth: In Lecture 14, focus on row/null and column/left-null orthogonality. The norm and angle calculations belong to the next unit.

study.title: Rank-nullity and orthogonal complements
study.locator: Chapter 2, section 2.7.3 (pp. 59 to 61), Theorem 2.24; Chapter 3, section 3.6 (pp. 79 to 80)

focus: For A in R^(m by n) of rank r, column and left-null spaces live in R^m with dimensions r and m-r. Row and null spaces live in R^n with dimensions r and n-r.
Prove rank-nullity by extending a basis of ker(A) to a domain basis; show that the images of the added vectors form a basis of im(A).
Each row dotted with x is a component of Ax. This gives ker(A)=row(A)^perp; apply the same argument to A^T for the other pair.
Ax=b is solvable iff b lies in col(A). When solvable, its full solution set is x_p+ker(A), so unique coefficients require full column rank.
units.reproduce: By hand use A=[[1,2,0],[0,0,1],[1,2,1]]. Find column basis {(1,0,1),(0,1,1)}, row basis {(1,2,0),(0,0,1)}, null basis {(-2,1,0)}, and left-null basis {(-1,-1,1)}. For b=(3,4,7), obtain all solutions (3,0,4)+t(-2,1,0). Changing b to (3,4,8) makes the system inconsistent. Write the basis-extension proof of rank-nullity. Check once in NumPy with all arrays dtype=np.float64 and no random draws: matrix_rank(A) gives 2; the vector 2-norms of A@(-2,1,0), A.T@(-1,-1,1), and A@(3,0,4)-b each give 0.0, below 1e-12. The left-null vector dotted with (3,4,8) gives approximately 1, certifying the hand inconsistency argument.
traps: Pivot columns must be taken from the original A to form a column-space basis. Row reduction preserves the row space and kernel, not the column space as a subset of R^m.
A tall matrix can have a unique solution for each attainable b without being surjective. Full column rank and full row rank answer different questions.
Numerical rank depends on a singular-value threshold. Do not confuse that decision with exact dependence in a symbolic matrix.

selfTest.q: Why are the images of the added basis vectors independent in the rank-nullity proof?
selfTest.a: A zero combination of their images puts the corresponding domain combination in ker(A). Express it in the chosen kernel basis. Independence of the extended domain basis then forces all added-vector coefficients to be zero. Finite dimension permits the basis extension; linearity moves the combination through A.

selfTest.q: When does a real m by n matrix give exactly one solution for every b in R^m?
selfTest.a: Existence for every b requires rank m; uniqueness requires rank n. Both imply m=n=rank(A), so A is square and invertible.

selfTest.q: Why is the full solution set x_p+ker(A), not span{x_p,ker(A)}?
selfTest.a: Linearity gives A(x_p+z)=b when Az=0. Conversely, any solution x satisfies A(x-x_p)=0. The coefficient of x_p is fixed at one unless b=0; scaling x_p generally scales b.

selfTest.q: How can a left-null vector disprove solvability?
selfTest.a: If A^T l=0, then l^T Ax=0 for every x. Thus l^T b must vanish for a solution to exist. For the worked matrix l=(-1,-1,1) and b=(3,4,8), it is 1, a contradiction.
